content_voiceover: McLeod syndrome is an even rarer example, an extremely rare blood type occurring far less than one in a thousand, more like one in a hundred thousand to one in a million. It's caused by mutation in the Xk gene on the X chromosome, at Xp21.1. Xk normally encodes the Kx antigen, which is linked by a disulfide bond to the Kell glycoprotein on the red cell membrane. Because it's X-linked, McLeod syndrome primarily affects males, and the disease itself is a form of neuroacanthocytosis, meaning patients develop neurologic and muscular symptoms alongside acanthocytes, spiky red cells, on the peripheral smear. The pedigree here shows a two-year-old boy who was previously transfused and subsequently developed anti-Kx and anti-Km antibodies in his serum, which makes finding compatible blood for future transfusions extremely difficult. As of now, only two McLeod families have been reported in Taiwan. Management strategies mirror other rare phenotypes, screening family members for the same variant and maintaining autologous frozen red cell units for the patient's own future use.
keypoints: McLeod syndrome: X-linked mutation in the Xk gene (Xp21.1), Kx antigen absent
Neuro-acanthocytosis: neuromuscular disease plus acanthocytes on smear, mainly affects males
Transfused patients can form anti-Kx/anti-Km -- compatible blood is extremely rare
Management: screen family members and store autologous frozen RBC units
